column1: count vs for_each - the real difference?
column2: count uses positional indexes so removing a middle element shifts everything after it (destroy+recreate). for_each uses stable string keys so removal affects exactly one resource.

column1: Two engineers apply at once - what happens?
column2: State locking makes one fail rather than corrupting state. In CI use a concurrency group with cancel-in-progress: false.

column1: Why cancel-in-progress: false on terraform CI?
column2: Cancelling a running apply leaves a stuck lock and possibly half-created infrastructure. Queue, never cancel.
Workspaces share one backend and one config - good for ephemeral identical copies. Directories give separate state and allow prod to genuinely differ. For real environments, use directories.

column1: GitHub OIDC to AWS - what claim does the trust policy check?
column2: The `sub` claim, e.g. repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main. PR runs have a different sub (repo:org/repo:pull_request).

column1: Risk of `sub: repo:org/repo:*` in a trust policy?
column2: Any branch in that repo can assume the role - so anyone who can open a PR reaches your AWS account. Pin production to environment:production.

column1: Terraform state lock stuck - correct order of action?
column2: 1) Confirm no apply is actually running. 2) terraform force-unlock <ID>. 3) Last resort: delete the DynamoDB lock item. Never force-unlock reflexively.
